{{Short description|Measure theory}}
{{No footnotes|date=June 2020}}
In [[mathematics]], the notions of '''prevalence and shyness''' are notions of "[[almost everywhere]]" and "[[measure zero]]" that are well-suited to the study of [[Infinity|infinite]]-[[dimension]]al spaces and make use of the translation-invariant [[Lebesgue measure]] on finite-dimensional real spaces. The term "shy" was suggested by the [[United States|American]] [[mathematician]] [[John Milnor]].

== Definitions ==

=== Prevalence and shyness ===

Let <math>V</math> be a [[Real number|real]] [[topological vector space]] and let <math>S</math> be a [[Borel sigma algebra|Borel-measurable]] [[subset]] of <math>V.</math> <math>S</math> is said to be '''prevalent''' if there exists a finite-dimensional subspace <math>P</math> of <math>V,</math> called the '''probe set''', such that for all <math>v \in V</math> we have <math>v + p \in S</math> for <math>\lambda_P</math>-[[almost all]] <math>p \in P,</math> where <math>\lambda_P</math> denotes the <math>\dim (P)</math>-dimensional Lebesgue measure on <math>P.</math> Put another way, for every <math>v \in V,</math> Lebesgue-almost every point of the [[hyperplane]] <math>v + P</math> lies in <math>S.</math>

A non-Borel subset of <math>V</math> is said to be prevalent if it contains a prevalent Borel subset.

A Borel subset of <math>V</math> is said to be '''shy''' if its [[Complement (set theory)|complement]] is prevalent; a non-Borel subset of <math>V</math> is said to be shy if it is contained within a shy Borel subset.

An alternative, and slightly more general, definition is to define a set <math>S</math> to be shy if there exists a [[transverse measure]] for <math>S</math> (other than the [[trivial measure]]).

=== Local prevalence and shyness ===

A subset <math>S</math> of <math>V</math> is said to be '''locally shy''' if every point <math>v \in V</math> has a [[Neighbourhood (topology)|neighbourhood]] <math>N_v</math> whose [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]] with <math>S</math> is a shy set. <math>S</math> is said to be '''locally prevalent''' if its complement is locally shy.

== Theorems involving prevalence and shyness ==

* If <math>S</math> is shy, then so is every subset of <math>S</math> and every translate of <math>S.</math>
* Every shy Borel set <math>S</math> admits a transverse measure that is finite and has [[Compact space|compact]] [[Support (measure theory)|support]]. Furthermore, this measure can be chosen so that its support has arbitrarily small [[diameter]].
* Any finite or [[countable]] [[Union (set theory)|union]] of shy sets is also shy. Analogously, countable intersection of prevalent sets is prevalent.
* Any shy set is also locally shy. If <math>V</math> is a [[separable space]], then every locally shy subset of <math>V</math> is also shy.
* A subset <math>S</math> of <math>n</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] <math>\R^n</math> is shy [[if and only if]] it has Lebesgue measure zero.
* Any prevalent subset <math>S</math> of <math>V</math> is [[Dense (topology)|dense]] in <math>V.</math>
* If <math>V</math> is infinite-dimensional, then every compact subset of <math>V</math> is shy.

In the following, "almost every" is taken to mean that the stated property holds of a prevalent subset of the space in question.

* Almost every [[continuous function]] from the [[Interval (mathematics)|interval]] <math>[0, 1]</math> into the [[real line]] <math>\R</math> is [[nowhere differentiable]]; here the space <math>V</math> is <math>C([0, 1]; \R)</math> with the topology induced by the [[supremum norm]].
* Almost every function <math>f</math> in the [[Lp space|<math>L^p</math> space]] <math>L^1([0, 1]; \R)</math> has the property that <math display=block>\int_0^1 f(x) \, \mathrm{d} x \neq 0.</math> Clearly, the same property holds for the spaces of <math>k</math>-times [[differentiable function]]s <math>C^k([0, 1]; \R).</math>
* For <math>1 < p \leq +\infty,</math> almost every sequence <math>a = \left(a_n\right)_{n \in \N} \in \ell^p</math> has the property that the series <math display=block>\sum_{n \in \N} a_n</math> diverges.
* Prevalence version of the [[Whitney embedding theorem]]: Let <math>M</math> be a compact [[manifold]] of class <math>C^1</math> and dimension <math>d</math> contained in <math>\R^n.</math>  For <math>1 \leq k \leq +\infty,</math> almost every <math>C^k</math> function <math>f : \R^n \to \R^{2d+1}</math> is an [[embedding]] of <math>M.</math>
* If <math>A</math> is a compact subset of <math>\R^n</math> with [[Hausdorff dimension]] <math>d,</math> <math>m \geq ,</math> and <math>1 \leq k \leq +\infty,</math> then, for almost every <math>C^k</math> function <math>f : \R^n \to \R^m,</math> <math>f(A)</math> also has Hausdorff dimension <math>d.</math>
* For <math>1 \leq k \leq +\infty,</math> almost every <math>C^k</math> function <math>f : \R^n \to \R^n</math> has the property that all of its [[periodic point]]s are hyperbolic. In particular, the same is true for all the period <math>p</math> points, for any integer <math>p.</math>
